core_summary: Surveys the long-term climatic patterns governing India over decades. Explores thermal differences driving the South-West and North-East monsoons, traditional six-season cycles (Ritus), regional climatic controls (latitude, altitude, continentality), and the severe socioeconomic disruptions caused by anthropogenic climate change and natural hazards.
key_concepts: Differential Thermal Heating: The physical principle that land surfaces absorb and radiate heat much faster than oceanic water bodies, driving global monsoon wind reversals.
Ritu Cycle & Bio-Rhythms: Traditional Indian calendar dividing the year into six two-month seasons (Vasanta, Grishma, Varsha, Sharad, Hemanta, Shishir) aligned with agricultural activities.
Continentality (Distance from Sea): The extreme temperature variations experienced in continental land interiors compared to milder maritime coastal climates.
Retreating North-East Monsoon: Winter wind reversal blowing from cold northern landmasses across the Bay of Bengal, delivering winter rain to southeastern coastal India.
Anthropogenic Global Warming: Enhanced greenhouse heat trapping resulting from fossil fuel combustion and widespread deforestation.

key_terms.definition: A measure of the difference between continental and marine climates, characterized by extreme seasonal temperature fluctuations far from oceans.
Traditional Indian season in the Hindu calendar, comprising six distinct seasonal periods throughout the year.
Precipitation produced when moist air is forced upward over a rising mountain barrier, condensing as it cools.
Actions and strategies designed to reduce or prevent emission of greenhouse gases to curb global warming.
The capacity of a community or ecosystem to anticipate, absorb, adapt to, and recover from climate-induced hazards.

key_takeaways: Monsoon winds are the primary economic driver of Indian agriculture, directly impacting crop yields, rural livelihoods, and national inflation.
India's regional climate ranges from alpine freezing in Leh to tropical moist conditions in coastal Tamil Nadu due to complex topographical controls.
Human-induced climate change increases the frequency and severity of extreme weather events like urban floods, cyclones, and glacial lake outbursts.
